passage:
You're looking at that forward about the other school, Elizabeth. I'm Vidya, and let me tell you what I did as a schoolgirl of sixteen.
We had phones with tiny screens then, only messages. One evening a text came: "St. Anne's got the quiz questions early. Their captain's uncle is a judge." We had lost to St. Anne's that week. I was so angry my hands shook. It felt true because we already felt cheated.
I didn't ask who wrote it. I sent it to twenty-three people. Sending it felt like standing up for my team.
By Monday it was everywhere. Their captain, a quiet girl called Rosalind, stopped coming to the inter-school events. Her uncle was not a judge. Nobody had checked.
I wrote her a note in December. She never answered. I don't blame her.
That's all, beta. Now tell me, who wrote the one on your phone?

qa.q: How many people did young Vidya send the message to?
qa.a: Vidya sent it to twenty-three people.

qa.q: Why did the message feel true to sixteen-year-old Vidya?
qa.a: Vidya was already angry about losing to St. Anne's, so a story that said they had cheated matched what she felt, and forwarding it felt like loyalty.

qa.q: At which point in the story could young Vidya have stopped the harm?
qa.a: When the text arrived, she could have asked who wrote it and whether the uncle was really a judge before sending it to anyone.

qa.q: What was it like for Rosalind once the message spread?
qa.a: Rosalind was blamed for something untrue and stopped coming to inter-school events, so the forward cost her a place she used to enjoy.

grounding: A woman recalls forwarding, at sixteen, an angry rumour about a rival school's captain because it fit what her team already felt.

passage:
It was 10:30 at night, the power had gone, and Mridul's phone was at 9 percent with a maths exam at eight the next morning.
Then the colony cricket group lit up. A blurry photo of their pitch, dug up in patches, and a message: "Green Park boys did this. Share everywhere, everyone should know."
Mridul's face went hot. Green Park had beaten them in the final and laughed about it. Of course it was them. His thumb was already forwarding it to the school group, then the tuition group. He felt like he was protecting his team.
Darshan messaged him privately. "Who took the photo? Whose pitch is that even?"
Mridul looked again by the light of a candle. The fence in the photo was blue. Theirs was green.
His battery hit 4 percent. He deleted the forwards he could and wrote, "Not sure this is our pitch, don't share." Then the screen went dark.

qa.q: What colour was the fence in the photo?
qa.a: The fence in the photo was blue.

qa.q: Why did Mridul forward the photo so fast?
qa.a: Mridul was angry at Green Park for beating his team and laughing, so the message fitted what he already felt and sharing it felt like protecting his side.

qa.q: Which choice helped Mridul stop the rumour, even in a hurry?
qa.a: Looking again after Darshan asked who took the photo, then deleting the forwards and warning others not to share, stopped it before his phone died.

qa.q: What would change for the Green Park boys if Mridul had not looked again?
qa.a: They might have been blamed across several groups for damage they may not have done, just because the story fitted an old rivalry.

grounding: A teenage boy angrily forwards a message blaming a rival team because it fits his group's feelings, then checks the source when questioned.

passage:
Thursday night
Our class group was already boiling about the quiz final. Then someone posted a screenshot: "St Anne's got the questions a day early, the quizmaster is their principal's cousin!!" My face went hot and I forwarded it to three more groups before I'd even finished reading. It felt like standing up for our team.
An hour later Vishal messaged me privately: "who made that screenshot?" I didn't know. Nobody knew. It had no name, no date, just angry capitals.
Then someone who actually knew replied: the quizmaster was a lecturer from a college in another city, with no link to St Anne's at all.
I felt stupid. Worse, I'd spread it. I posted "I shared this without checking, sorry, please don't forward" in all three groups. Two people left laughing reactions. It still stings. But Vishal sent a 🙏.
Sarika

qa.q: What did the screenshot claim about St Anne's?
qa.a: That St Anne's got the questions a day early and the quizmaster is their principal's cousin.

qa.q: Why did Sarika forward the screenshot so fast?
qa.a: Sarika was angry along with the class, and forwarding felt like standing up for the team, so loyalty came before checking.

qa.q: What did Sarika do after learning the truth, and what could come first next time?
qa.a: Sarika posted a correction in all three groups; next time, asking who made the message before forwarding, as Vishal did, would stop it earlier.

qa.q: How might students at St Anne's feel seeing the screenshot spread?
qa.a: They would likely feel unfairly accused, since the claim had no name or date and turned out to be false.

grounding: Shows a teenager forwarding an unsourced accusation because it fit the class's anger, sharing out of loyalty before checking.

passage:
The tournament final in Kherwadi was two days away when the voice note reached Anand's phone: a man's angry voice saying Rampur's team had brought in three college players "with fake certificates". Anand felt his chest tighten. Rampur had beaten them last year too. Before dinner he forwarded it to the village youth group and the family group. Uncles replied with angry faces. Someone typed that Rampur always cheats.
His cousin Avni came in with the milk. "Who's the man in the voice note?"
"Doesn't matter. Everyone knows it's true."
"I'll ask Sharma sir, he's organising." She called right there. The players' ages had been checked against school records on Monday. All fine.
Anand stared at the family group, where his message sat at the top. "If I say it's wrong now, they'll say I'm on Rampur's side," he muttered. Then, slowly, he typed the correction.

qa.q: What did the voice note claim about Rampur's team?
qa.a: That Rampur's team had brought in three college players 'with fake certificates'.

qa.q: Why did Anand forward the voice note so quickly?
qa.a: Anand felt angry and still stung by last year's loss to Rampur, so a message that matched that feeling seemed true without checking.

qa.q: Which step did Avni take that Anand could use before forwarding?
qa.a: Asking who made the voice note and calling the organiser, Sharma sir, who confirmed the ages had been checked.

qa.q: How might Rampur's players feel if the correction never came?
qa.a: They would be called cheats across the village for something false, and the final could turn hostile.

grounding: Shows a teenager forwarding an anonymous accusation against a rival village team because it fits local anger, then correcting it.

passage: Zanele was on the minibus home in Johannesburg when the message landed in her class group: a blurry photo and the words, "Kids from Westridge High trashed our field last night. Share so everyone knows what they're like!" Her face went hot. Westridge had beaten them in the netball final and laughed about it. Of course it was them. Without a second look, she forwarded it to three more groups and added, "Typical." It felt good, like standing up for her school. By the time she got home it was everywhere. Then Rafael texted her: "That photo's from a news story two years ago, different city. My brother looked it up." Zanele stared at the screen. She hadn't even wondered where it came from. Her stomach dropped. She had wanted it to be true so badly. She typed into each group: "I shared this without checking. It's an old photo from somewhere else. Sorry."

qa.q: What did the message claim Westridge kids had done?
qa.a: Trashed their field last night.

qa.q: Why did forwarding the message feel good to Zanele?
qa.a: Zanele felt angry at Westridge after the netball final, and sharing felt loyal, like standing up for her school.

qa.q: What did Zanele do to repair it, and what could she do next time?
qa.a: She posted a correction in each group; next time she could ask where a photo came from before sharing, especially when it makes her angry.

qa.q: How might Westridge students feel about the message?
qa.a: They would likely feel hurt and unfairly blamed for something they didn't do, while the photo spread across many groups.

grounding: Shows a teenager forwarding a shocking message because it fits what her group already feels, without checking the source while angry.
